abstract.t: This document specifies the Secure Transport Communication Protocol (STCP). Its intended status is Standards Track. This document records the current STCP wire protocol and implementation observations to support experimentation and interoperability review. It does not claim complete cross-platform interoperability, Internet-wide UDP congestion safety, or peer identity authentication.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: STCP is a transport protocol with compact framing, X25519 key establishment, and AES-256-GCM-protected data and control messages. The wire version is distinct from the product version.

section.name: Requirements Language
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 ( and ) when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

This initial draft also records implementation observations and explicitly identified open design questions. Descriptions of current Linux behavior are not automatically normative requirements for independent implementations.

section.name: Architecture and Transport Mapping
section.t: STCP is a distinct framed and encrypted protocol implemented above an underlying TCP or UDP transport. The reviewed Linux implementation registers its own socket family and socket operations, but uses a kernel-created TCP or UDP socket as the carrier for each STCP connection. STCP does not implement a native IP carrier.

section.name: Linux Socket API Mapping (Implementation-Specific)
section.t: The reviewed Linux kernel module defines AF_STCP and PF_STCP as 45. The protocol argument to socket() selects the STCP carrier: STCP_PROTO_DEFAULT (0) and STCP_PROTO_TCP (253) select TCP, while STCP_PROTO_UDP (254) selects UDP. These constants are Linux implementation API selectors; they are not assigned IP Protocol or IPv6 Next Header values and do not appear in the outer IP header as STCP protocol numbers. The implementation registers a struct proto with proto_register(), a struct net_proto_family with sock_register(), and its own struct proto_ops including bind, connect, listen, accept, sendmsg, recvmsg, poll, shutdown, and socket-option callbacks. This section describes the implementation and does not require other operating systems to adopt Linux numeric constants or APIs.

section.name: TCP and UDP Carriers
section.t: The Linux carrier creates an internal IPv4 socket using sock_create_kern() with IPPROTO_TCP for TCP mode or IPPROTO_UDP for UDP mode. Consequently, packets sent by these carriers use the ordinary outer IP protocol values TCP (6) and UDP (17), respectively. The STCP wire framing, handshake, and authenticated messages are transported within the selected carrier. TCP provides its own reliable ordered byte stream and congestion control. UDP provides datagrams; STCP's UDP reliability and congestion behavior must be specified independently. The STCP protocol argument supplied to socket(AF_STCP, ...) is not the outer IP Protocol field.

section.name: Wire Format
section.t: Each frame starts with a 17-octet header. Octet 0 is the descriptor: bits 0-3 packet type, bits 4-5 wire version (3), and bits 6-7 flags. Octets 1-4 contain the payload length; octets 5-8 the sequence; octets 9-12 the acknowledgment; and octets 13-16 the connection ID. All multioctet integers are big-endian.

Packet types are PublicKey (1), HandshakeDone (2), DataChunk (3), DataChunkEnd (4), Ack (5), Ping (6), Pong (7), Close (8), and Reset (9). PublicKey has a 64-octet payload; HandshakeDone has no payload. The implementation rejects unknown versions and packet types.

section.name: Framing over TCP and UDP
section.t: STCP uses the same 17-octet header and length-delimited frame encoding over both supported carriers. The payload length at header offsets 1 through 4 is an unsigned 32-bit integer in network byte order and counts the octets following the header. The complete frame length is therefore 17 plus the encoded payload length. A receiver MUST validate the descriptor, frame type, and applicable length bounds before consuming the complete frame.

section.name: TCP Byte-Stream Mapping
section.t: TCP carries an ordered byte stream without application message boundaries. An STCP frame is serialized as its 17-octet header immediately followed by the number of payload octets indicated by that header; successive frames are concatenated without a separate carrier-level delimiter or length prefix. A TCP read can contain a partial header, a partial payload, one frame, or portions of multiple frames. The STCP receiver buffers incomplete data and MUST NOT interpret a frame until its complete header and payload have arrived. The current Linux implementation uses a bounded receive queue, peeks at the header when 17 octets are available, and waits until the complete frame length is buffered. Its TCP carrier loops over partial kernel_sendmsg() results until all submitted bytes have been sent or a terminal error occurs.

section.name: UDP Datagram Mapping
section.t: UDP carries datagrams rather than a reliable ordered stream. The current Linux UDP carrier passes each received datagram and its peer IPv4 address and UDP port to the STCP Rust receive path. The listener uses the STCP connection ID in the first complete header to find or create a per-peer session; a new session is admitted only from a PublicKey frame with a complete 64-octet key payload, and packets from an unexpected source address or port for an existing session are discarded. UDP transmission uses kernel_sendmsg() for a datagram and treats a partial send as an error. The precise requirements for one versus multiple STCP frames per UDP datagram, datagram truncation, and malformed trailing bytes remain to be made normative after verification across all implementations; this draft does not yet assert a one-frame-per-datagram rule.

section.name: Implementation Frame Bounds
section.t: The reviewed Rust implementation defines a 60-KiB UDP DATA payload target and a 2-MiB stream DATA payload target, with an 8-octet transmitted nonce and 16-octet authentication tag. The decoder also applies packet-type-specific payload bounds: PublicKey is at most 64 octets, HandshakeDone is empty, and protected control frames are at most 24 octets. These values describe implementation behavior; negotiated and interoperable maximum-frame-size requirements remain open.

section.name: Handshake and State Transitions
section.t: The implementation states are New, Bound, Listening, Handshake, Ready, Closed, and Error. The handshake procedures described below are observed in the 2026-11-02 Linux source snapshot; complete wire-level error semantics are not yet standardized.

li.t: When a connection enters Handshake with an attached carrier, the local endpoint sends a PublicKey frame. Its 64-octet payload contains the local 32-octet X25519 public key in octets 0 through 31. The current Linux implementation initializes the remaining 32 octets to zero. The PublicKey frame advertises the COMPRESSION_CAPABLE flag.

On receiving a PublicKey frame, the implementation requires a 64-octet payload and rejects flags other than COMPRESSION_CAPABLE. It derives directional traffic keys from the peer public key and sends an empty HandshakeDone frame.

The receiver permits HandshakeDone to arrive before PublicKey and remembers its receipt. The handshake parser stops before consuming subsequent application DATA when the required handshake inputs are present.

The local connection transitions to Ready only when local traffic keys have been derived and a peer HandshakeDone has been received. An established application DATA frame must not be interpreted as a handshake frame.

section.t: PublicKey and HandshakeDone are not protected by the established-session DATA or control authentication mechanism. In particular, HandshakeDone does not prove the peer's identity or cryptographically bind the full handshake transcript. The base protocol does not authenticate peer identity.

section.name: Directional Key Derivation
section.t: The active Linux key derivation takes the 32-octet X25519 shared secret, the 32-octet client public key, and the 32-octet server public key, in that role-defined order. It computes:

li.t: client_to_server_key = HMAC-SHA256(key=PRK, message=ASCII("STCPv4 AES256-GCM client to server key") || 0x01).
server_to_client_key = HMAC-SHA256(key=PRK, message=ASCII("STCPv4 AES256-GCM server to client key") || 0x01).
For each direction, control_key = HMAC-SHA256(key=directional_data_key, message=ASCII("STCP wire3 control AES256-GCM key") || 0x01).

section.t: ASCII strings do not include a terminating NUL octet. The client uses the client-to-server key for transmission and the server-to-client key for reception; the server uses the reverse assignment. The reviewed code rejects identical directional keys. A separate STCPv2 derivation helper exists in the source tree but is not invoked by this reviewed Linux session-key path. Cross-platform equivalence and deterministic known-answer vectors remain to be verified.

section.name: Packet Protection
section.t: DATA uses AES-256-GCM with the encoded 17-octet header as additional authenticated data, an 8-octet transmitted nonce, and a 16-octet tag. The 12-octet GCM IV is four zero octets followed by the big-endian transmitted nonce. Control packets Ack, Ping, Pong, Close, and Reset use a separate derived control key and authenticate the header with a tag over empty plaintext. A 64-position replay window rejects duplicate authenticated control nonces.

section.name: Authenticated Packet Layout and Replay Handling
section.t: For encrypted DATA, the 17-octet encoded header is AES-GCM additional authenticated data (AAD). The frame carries an 8-octet big-endian nonce followed by ciphertext and a 16-octet authentication tag. The 12-octet GCM IV is 0x00000000 || nonce. Reliable retransmission reuses the original stored encrypted frame bytes instead of encrypting altered plaintext under the same nonce.

A protected control frame (Ack, Ping, Pong, Close, or Reset) uses a distinct directional control key, its encoded header as AAD, an 8-octet nonce, and a 16-octet authentication tag over empty plaintext. After tag verification, the receiver applies a 64-position sliding replay window: duplicates and values at least 64 behind the greatest accepted nonce are rejected. In-order DATA delivery also checks the expected sequence and nonce after authentication; authenticated out-of-order DATA can be buffered.
These observations do not establish nonce uniqueness across every reconnect, failure, alternate carrier, or key-lifecycle path.

section.name: Reliability, Acknowledgments and Retransmission
section.t: The following values describe the reviewed Linux implementation rather than negotiated protocol parameters. Reliability is enabled when the carrier reports that STCP reliability is required; the TCP carrier does not run the STCP retransmission timer.

section.name: Send Window and Segmentation
section.t: The implementation uses a fixed maximum of eight outstanding reliable DATA frames per connection. An application send that would exceed the pending-frame limit returns a retry indication instead of adding the frames. Application data is split into DataChunk frames, with DataChunkEnd marking the last frame of a send. This limit is a frame-count bound, not a receiver-advertised congestion window.

section.name: Cumulative ACK Processing
section.t: ACK values are cumulative. On receipt of a valid authenticated ACK with acknowledgment number A, the sender removes pending frames whose sequence numbers are less than or equal to A. An ACK referring to a sequence not yet transmitted is treated as a protocol error. The receiver normally sends an ACK after four received frames; selected events can force an earlier ACK. Duplicate-ACK recovery can resend the latest cumulative acknowledgment. When acknowledged frames release pending capacity, blocked senders are awakened.

section.name: Round-Trip Time Estimation
section.t: The initial retransmission timeout (RTO) is 60 milliseconds. The timer tick is 20 milliseconds, and the RTO is clamped between 20 and 3000 milliseconds. An RTT sample is collected only from a frame that has not been retransmitted, avoiding ambiguous samples as in Karn's algorithm. On the first sample R, SRTT is R and RTTVAR is max(1, floor(R/2)). On subsequent samples, RTTVAR becomes floor((3*RTTVAR + abs(SRTT-R))/4) and SRTT becomes floor((7*SRTT + R)/8). RTO becomes clamp(SRTT + 4*RTTVAR, 20, 3000) milliseconds. These integer formulas reflect the current implementation.

section.name: Retransmission Timer
section.t: For each pending frame, the implementation maintains an age in timer ticks, a per-frame RTO and a retry count. On expiry it resends the stored encrypted frame bytes without generating a new nonce. Per-frame RTO doubles after a retransmission, capped at 3000 milliseconds. No more than four pending frames are selected for retransmission per timer tick. After eight retries for a pending frame, the connection reports a terminal timeout corresponding to ETIMEDOUT. The implementation updates retransmission and timeout counters.

section.name: Congestion-Control Limitations
section.t: The fixed eight-frame outstanding limit and four-retransmissions-per-tick bound limit bursts, but do not establish a complete Internet congestion-control algorithm. No standards-conformant congestion response to sustained loss, fairness mechanism, or explicit receiver-advertised flow-control window has yet been verified from the reviewed source. When STCP is carried over TCP, congestion control and transport backpressure are provided by the underlying TCP connection; the STCP retransmission timer is not used for that carrier. For STCP over UDP, the fixed outstanding-frame limit is not a substitute for a validated congestion-control algorithm. Direct STCP carriage over IP is not implemented in the current version and is outside the scope of this specification. Congestion behavior for UDP carriage requires further validation before Standards Track readiness.

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: STCP deliberately does not provide peer identity authentication in its base protocol and does not require persistent authentication keys, a public-key infrastructure, or an identity-key distribution mechanism. X25519 establishes ephemeral shared key material and AES-256-GCM protects subsequent encrypted frames, but neither operation authenticates the identity of the remote endpoint. An active man-in-the-middle can substitute handshake public keys and establish separate encrypted sessions with both endpoints. Applications requiring authenticated peer identity MUST provide an appropriate authentication mechanism outside this base protocol and MUST NOT treat successful STCP key establishment as proof of peer identity. The connection ID is not an authentication credential.

Implementations MUST terminate the affected connection when a fatal cryptographic validation failure, unrecoverable protocol violation, or irrecoverably inconsistent connection state is detected; they MUST NOT continue processing application data in an uncertain cryptographic or protocol state. Ordinary packet loss, reordering, and retransmission within the defined reliability behavior are not by themselves fatal protocol violations. This fail-closed requirement does not prescribe a particular operating-system error code or internal implementation state.

Nonce uniqueness, session-key freshness, reconnect behavior, and cross-platform interoperability require further verification. This initial specification does not claim resistance to active handshake interception or general Internet deployment safety for UDP carriage.

section.name: IANA Considerations
section.t: This initial version requests no allocation. The Linux STCP_PROTO_TCP value 253 and STCP_PROTO_UDP value 254 are local AF_STCP socket API selectors, not allocations in the IP Protocol Numbers registry. IP protocol number 253 is reserved for experimentation and is not a permanent STCP assignment. Direct STCP carriage over IP is not currently implemented and is outside the scope of this draft. No permanent IP protocol number is requested. Any future native-IP specification and allocation request require separate work.

section.name: Outstanding Work
section.t: For broader interoperable deployment, the draft still needs complete normative state-machine and error rules, independent KDF test vectors, verified carrier mapping, compression negotiation, UDP congestion control, security review, and cross-platform interoperability evidence. This document does not claim IETF approval.
